questions.question: Which of these triggers the execution of a Spark job?
options: `df.filter(...)`
`df.select(...)`
`df.count()`
`df.withColumn(...)`
questions.explanation: Transformations (filter, select, withColumn, join…) are lazy: they only build a plan. Actions (count, collect, show, write) trigger execution, which lets Spark optimize the whole plan at once.

questions.question: Which operation causes a shuffle (data exchanged between executors)?
options: `filter`
`select`
`groupBy(...).agg(...)`
`withColumn`
questions.explanation: Wide transformations (groupBy, distinct, most joins, repartition) need all rows with the same key on the same partition, so data moves across the network. Narrow ones (filter, select, map) work partition by partition.

questions.question: You join a 2 TB fact table with a 20 MB country table. What does a broadcast join do?
options: Sends a copy of the small table to every executor, so the big table is not shuffled
Splits both tables into equal partitions
Writes the small table to disk first
Sorts both tables before merging them
questions.explanation: Every executor joins its partitions of the big table locally with its copy of the small one, which avoids shuffling 2 TB. Spark does it automatically below `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold`, or when you use the `broadcast()` hint.

questions.question: In a stage, 199 tasks finish in seconds and one runs for 20 minutes. What is the likely cause, and a fix?
options: Data skew on the join or group key; salt the key or enable AQE skew-join handling
Not enough memory on the driver; increase driver memory
Too many partitions; call `coalesce(1)`
The cluster is too big; remove executors
questions.explanation: One key (often NULL or a default value) holds a large share of the rows, so its partition becomes a straggler. Salting spreads that key over several partitions; Adaptive Query Execution can split skewed partitions automatically.

questions.question: What is the difference between `repartition(n)` and `coalesce(n)`?
options: None, they are aliases
`coalesce` reduces the number of partitions by merging them without a full shuffle; `repartition` does a full shuffle and can increase or decrease it
`repartition` only works on RDDs
`coalesce` sorts the data
questions.explanation: `coalesce` is cheap for reducing partitions before a write, but it can leave them unbalanced. `repartition` rebalances evenly (optionally by column) at the cost of a shuffle.

questions.question: Why is writing 100,000 tiny Parquet files a problem?
options: Parquet does not support small files
Listing and opening many files adds large overhead, and small files compress and scan poorly
It uses too much driver memory during the write only
It is not a problem
questions.explanation: Readers spend their time on metadata and file opens instead of reading data. Fix it by repartitioning before writing, or by compacting regularly (e.g. `OPTIMIZE` on Delta tables).

questions.question: What does Parquet bring over CSV for analytics? Select all that apply.
options: Column pruning: read only the needed columns
Efficient per-column compression and encoding
An embedded schema with real data types
Files that are easy to read in a text editor
questions.explanation: Parquet is columnar, compressed and typed, and it stores statistics that allow predicate pushdown (skipping row groups). It is binary, so it is not human-readable.

questions.question: When is `df.cache()` worth using?
options: Always, it makes every job faster
When the same DataFrame is reused by several actions
Before writing a DataFrame once
To reduce the number of partitions
questions.explanation: Without caching, every action recomputes the lineage from the source. Caching pays off when a result is reused; otherwise it just consumes executor memory.

questions.question: An action is called on a DataFrame. Order what Spark does.
steps: The driver builds a logical plan from your code
The Catalyst optimizer turns it into an optimized physical plan
The plan is split into stages at shuffle boundaries
Each stage is split into tasks, one per partition
Executors run the tasks and return or write the results
questions.explanation: Stages are separated by shuffles; within a stage, tasks run in parallel, one per partition. That is why the number of partitions sets the parallelism.

questions.question: A Spark job suddenly takes 3 hours instead of 20 minutes. Order the investigation.
steps: Open the Spark UI and find the slowest stage
Look at the task duration distribution to spot skew
Check shuffle read/write sizes and disk spill
Apply a targeted fix: broadcast join, salting, repartitioning, more memory
Re-run and compare the stage metrics
questions.explanation: The Spark UI shows where the time goes. Straggler tasks point to skew, and large spill points to memory or partition sizing, so you fix the actual bottleneck rather than guessing.
